title: What Do You Do Without Even Trying?
essay_markdown:
What do people thank you for that felt, to you, like nothing? Start there. It's often where your strengths are hiding.

## Strengths that look like quirks

Maggie Romanovich, a Training and Development professional, describes her own case this way on the Happen to Your Career podcast: "I have strengths that I've always viewed as, like, weird quirks, but they work really well in the job I'm at." Her former team leader had a name for them: "Maggie magic."

Romanovich moved into Training and Development to support sales teams, then rose through higher Training, Learning, and Development leadership roles. The host counts four promotions, including the career change, all in work that draws on her strengths. The traits she once dismissed as oddities turned out to be the engine of her career.

Actor Kim Jae-won gave a different kind of answer. Asked by Sports Kyunghyang about his strengths, he said: "I do not do anything half-heartedly." He calls it passion, and says it drives both his work as MC of KBS2's *Music Bank* and his attempts to play characters he hasn't shown before. He named a second strength too, one that came from experience: "Perhaps because I have worked with adults and been part of society since I was young, I am somewhat perceptive. I know how to grasp the subtext when they say something."

Notice that neither strength is a technical credential. One is a way of showing up. The other is a skill his circumstances trained into him.

## Know it, then build on it

The idea is simple: find out what you're good at, then put more of your effort there, not less. A strength can be a single sharp skill, or it can be a combination. Perceptiveness plus full commitment is a different asset than either alone. Plenty of people aren't the best in the room at any one thing, yet nobody else has their particular mix.

Building on a strength means treating it as something that compounds. If you're good at explaining things, you can get better at it, and then take on work where explaining is the whole point. Effort spent sharpening what already works usually pays back faster than effort spent patching what doesn't.

The catch is that strengths are hard to see from the inside. What comes easily to you feels ordinary, so you assume it's ordinary to everyone. Romanovich called hers quirks for exactly that reason.

## Try this today

Look for evidence instead of guessing:

- **Check the pattern.** Think of the last few times someone asked for your help, or praised something you barely noticed doing. What did those moments share?
- **Name the stack.** Write down two or three things you do well, then ask what happens when they combine. Careful plus friendly. Quick with numbers plus good at calming people down.
- **Aim it.** Pick one task this week where that combination could matter, and deliberately lean on it instead of doing the task the way you think you're supposed to.

Then, if you want to keep going, ask: how could I do more of this?

## One small thing for today

Text one colleague or friend and ask: "What's something you'd come to me for?" Write down the answer, even if it surprises you. It may be your own version of Maggie magic.

item.title: Build on your strengths
item.body: Know your strengths. What are you good at? How can you build on them to become even better at what you do? How can you leverage on your strengths to perform at work and in life? Your strength can be in a specific skill or the result of having a unique stack of skills.
